title: Can AI schedule production while your planner stays in charge?
description: What AI scheduling software does and what stays with your planner. We priced 12 tools and show how to test one on your past weeks.
verdict: Software proposes the schedule; your planner approves it. Fights over planner control are a key reason scheduling software fails.[^1][^2]
Fix routings and run times first. One NIST-backed shop did, and lead time fell from 12-14 weeks to five.[^3][^4]
Chatbots alone can't build a schedule you can run. Benchmarks show language models break capacity rules without a solver checking.[^5][^6]
Only seven of 12 tools publish a price. By our math, a 100-person shop's year one ran $2,940 to $25,000.[^24][^8]
Planners shift to exceptions and what-ifs. Where AI changed tasks, two in three firms used it only to help staff.[^9][^10]

summary: AI scheduling software books work within each machine's real hours, then re-plans when a machine breaks or a rush order lands.[^11][^12] What changes: your planner approves and adjusts schedules instead of building them, cutting weekly scheduling from 4 hours to 40 minutes in one vendor case.[^2][^19]
humanRole: Planner: approves every schedule before release and can override any move, with the reason logged. In one field study, schedulers ignored machine-made assignments that came with no explanation.[^4][^2]

Supervisor: confirms what the floor can really run today (people, tooling, material) before dispatch. Research treats planning, scheduling and dispatching as separate jobs with separate owners.[^9][^14]
Operations manager: sets the rules the software follows. These include the frozen window (the next hours or days nobody changes), the priority rule and overtime limits.[^15][^16]
You choose how much the software decides. A usability study found decision support improved schedules, and recommends letting users pick the level of automation.[^17]
teamAfter: Planners move from building the schedule to working exceptions: late orders, material gaps and what to tell customers.[^9] At Dauper, a monthly schedule fell from 2-5 days to about 10 minutes, per Siemens' own case study.[^18]
Planners test what-ifs before the week starts: overtime, a split batch, a second shift. At Vetnil, weekly scheduling fell from 4 hours to 40 minutes, per Siemens' case study.[^19]
More work can stay in-house. Artis Matriz, an 80-person maker, raised internal resource use from 65% to 85% and outsourced less, per Siemens' case study.[^20]
Most firms keep their people. Where AI changed tasks, 66% of firms only used it to help staff, and AI-related employment fell at 2%.[^10]

example.input: Illustrative example, not data. A 100-person job shop has 140 open work orders, routings for 15 work centers, a changeover matrix, shift calendars and material arrival dates.[^3] On Tuesday at 10:00, CNC (computer-controlled) machine 3 goes down for about 6 hours, and sales adds a rush order of 2,000 brackets due Friday.
example.output: The software proposes a new sequence, keeps the next 24 hours frozen, and moves nine jobs from CNC 3 to CNCs 4 and 5.[^16][^21] It flags three late orders and costs two fixes: 6 hours of Saturday overtime on CNC 4, or splitting the rush order. The planner picks one, notes why and releases it, and supervisors get the new dispatch list.[^4][^9]

tables.title: Can a chatbot build your schedule on its own?
tables.intro: No, not on its own: in 2026 research benchmarks, language models alone broke scheduling rules or failed to beat simple dispatching rules.[^5][^39] Language models do best writing and explaining a schedule, with a solver checking that it can run.[^6][^38]

rows.name: SCHEDBench (2026)
cells: 13 language models on 1,132 scheduling problems[^5]
They "largely fail"; rewording a prompt changes whether rules are met[^5]

rows.name: DynaSchedBench (2026)
cells: AI agents re-planning as disruptions arrive[^39]
Most fail to beat strong simple dispatching rules consistently[^39]

rows.name: Job-shop study, J. Manufacturing Systems (2026)
cells: Language models building job-shop schedules[^6]
Plain models give "fluent but physically infeasible" schedules; with checks, 97% were valid[^6]

rows.name: Solver-writing agent (Nov 2026)
cells: An AI agent that writes a solver, against one that schedules directly[^38]
Writing the solver was repeatable. Scheduling directly cost $2-23 a schedule and varied run to run[^38]

recipes.name: 1. Small shop, one planner, an ERP that already schedules (about 40-100 staff)
recipes.when: One bottleneck, a planner on a spreadsheet or whiteboard, and an ERP with finite loading you haven't switched on.[^26]
flow: Planner and supervisor: check routings, setup and run times for the 20 parts that take the most hours[^3]
Planner: set ERP shift calendars to match real shifts and planned maintenance[^13]
Planner: run the finite schedule weekly, freeze the near term (say, 2 days), and re-run only on real events[^16][^21]
Operations manager: review on-time delivery and changeover hours each week[^40]
recipes.cost: By our math, year-one list licenses for 5 office users run about $2,940 (MRPeasy Starter) to $6,600 (Business Central Premium).[^24][^25] Odoo lists per-user prices too, but we couldn't open its live page to confirm them.[^7]

recipes.name: 2. Mid-size plant with many changeovers and disruptions (about 100-500 staff)
recipes.when: Many changeovers, frequent rush orders or breakdowns, and an ERP scheduler your planners don't trust.
flow: Operations manager: write down the rules (priority rule, frozen window, overtime limits)[^15]
IT or ERP admin: connect the scheduler to the ERP for orders, routings and inventory[^30]
Planner: run it daily, and approve or override each proposal with a reason[^17][^4]
Supervisor: work from the dispatch list and report actual times back
recipes.cost: By our math, SkyPlanner for 15 work centers comes to about €4,788 a year, and EDGEBIC is a $25,000 one-time license.[^29][^8] PlanetTogether quotes about 4-8 weeks to integrate but shows no price.[^30]

recipes.name: 3. Data-rich plant with unusual rules: build on a free solver
recipes.when: Clean ERP or shop-floor data, odd constraints (tooling, operator skills, cure times), and someone who can maintain a model.[^41][^42]
flow: Data or IT lead: model routings and calendars in OR-Tools or Timefold[^41][^42]
Planner: rank the goals (late orders first, then changeovers) and check output daily[^4]
AI assistant: explains changes in plain words and drafts what-ifs, while the solver checks every schedule[^6][^38]
Operations manager: review schedule stability and on-time delivery monthly[^15]
recipes.cost: The solvers are free: OR-Tools and Timefold are Apache 2.0, frePPLe Community is MIT.[^41][^42][^32] The cost is staff time, and bought tools reach deployment about 67% of the time[^43], twice the internal-build rate.[^44]

rules.what: Manufacturing is covered, for employers with 100+ staff worldwide and 50+ covered employees.[^49] Shifts need 14 days' notice, and late changes owe predictability pay.[^49][^50] If software moves people's shifts, keep a person's time-stamped approval.[^50]

howToTest: Record your before numbers for 8-12 weeks: on-time delivery, changeover hours, overtime, schedule changes per week, planner hours and work in progress.[^40]
Pilot one line or cell first: pick 4-6 past weeks that had real disruptions. Freeze the data exactly as it stood on each Monday.
Replay those weeks in the tool and compare with what really happened and with a simple rule such as earliest due date. AI agents often fail to beat strong simple rules, so the rule is the bar.[^39]
Count capacity, calendar and material violations in every schedule. Language-model schedules often read well and still can't run.[^5][^6]
Count how many operations moved between runs; inside the frozen window it should be zero. Rescheduling more often than disruptions happen only makes the floor nervous.[^21][^15]
Run it in shadow for 4 weeks: the planner approves or overrides, with a reason for each override. Those reasons point to bad data and missing rules.[^4][^51]
Price the lift from your own books: changeover hours saved times your machine-hour cost, plus overtime and expedited freight avoided. Use your own rates, not published ones.
Decide at 90 days: compare against your before numbers from step 1.
watchOuts: Bad master data gives a confident, wrong schedule; in one study, system times didn't match the floor.[^4][^3] Audit routings for your top-hours parts before go-live.
Shadow spreadsheets: after go-live, firms reported running parallel systems and getting incorrect plans.[^51] Retire the spreadsheet on a set date and log overrides inside the tool.

Planners lose their say: fights over shop-floor control explain failed projects, and unexplained assignments get ignored.[^1][^4] Keep the planner's override and make the tool show why it moved each job.
Schedule churn: re-running on every blip unsettles the floor.[^21][^15] Freeze the near term and patch small events instead of rebuilding the whole plan.[^16]
Calendars that don't match shifts: finite capacity goes wrong when shift changes aren't modeled.[^13] Load real shift calendars, planned maintenance included.
Vendor numbers without methods[^23]: product pages claim gains like +50% on-time delivery and show no method.[^22] Test on your own past weeks before you sign.

faq.a: Not by itself, because benchmarks show language models break capacity rules and fail to beat simple dispatching rules.[^5][^39] Use scheduling software or a solver, and let AI explain the changes.[^6][^38]

faq.q: How much does production scheduling software cost?
faq.a: For a 100-person shop, year-one list licenses ran from about $2,940 to a $25,000 one-time license, by our math.[^24][^8] Seven of the 12 tools we read publish a price, and the rest quote.[^30][^31]

faq.q: How is an APS different from ERP scheduling?
faq.a: An ERP plans what to make and when material arrives, while an APS (advanced planning and scheduling tool) sequences every operation within real machine hours.[^52][^11] An APS also re-plans after disruptions.[^12]

faq.q: Can it build a schedule straight from my ERP?
faq.a: Yes, if the routings, run times and calendars in the ERP are correct.[^3][^13] The planner still approves the result.[^4]
Data clean-up comes first, then about 4-8 weeks for many integrations, by PlanetTogether's own claim.[^3][^30] Research calls these projects complex and risky.[^2]

faq.q: What data does scheduling software need?
faq.a: Open orders with due dates, routings with setup and run times, changeover times, shift calendars and material arrival dates.[^11][^30] It also needs actual times reported back from the floor.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when you run one ERP, a standard job-shop or flow setup, and have no in-house optimization skills. Most firms buy: 76% of enterprise AI use cases are now bought.[^53] Bought tools succeed about twice as often as internal builds.[^44]
buyVsBuild.build: Build when your rules are unusual (tooling, skills, cure times), your data is clean and someone can maintain the model. Free solvers ship job-shop examples: OR-Tools and Timefold.[^41][^42] AI can help write the solver, which proved more repeatable than AI as the scheduler.[^38]

pickElse: One bottleneck drives everything: pace the plant to it with Drum-Buffer-Rope from the Theory of Constraints before buying software.[^54]
Steady repeat demand: level the mix (heijunka) and pull with kanban instead of scheduling every job.[^55]
Lead times swing because of material, not machines: look at DDMRP, which plans around stock buffers.[^56]
Routings and run times are wrong: start with your state's NIST MEP center, as Stainless Works did before scheduling.[^57][^3]

sources.name: Fortune, MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing (18 Aug 2025)
sources.what: Fortune's write-up of MIT NANDA's The GenAI Divide report. Headline: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing; about 5% of AI pilot programs achieve rapid revenue acceleration, while the vast majority stall with little to no measurable P&L impact. Purchasing AI tools from specialized vendors and building partnerships succeed about 67% of the time. Its comparison for internal builds misstates the report, where internal builds reach deployment about a third of the time: cite this write-up for the 67% and its headline figures only; MIT's report carries the internal-build rate and the "twice" comparison. Read 28 Nov 2026.

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (Jul 2025)
sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

offer.heading: Bring us one bad week of your schedule
offer.body: Bring your scheduling process and one past week that went wrong. In 30 minutes you leave with the first step, a before-and-after measure and the data to fix first. No sales pitch.

reviews.notes: Wanted the before-and-after measure named and the decision point dated. The first test step now says these are your before numbers, and the last step decides at 90 days against them. Every recipe step already names its role.
Stalled on two terms: frozen window and finite loading. Both are now defined in plain words where they first appear. APS is defined in the FAQ, and WIP is spelled out as work in progress.

Asked whether one line can pilot first and how the gain hits margin. The test now starts with one line or cell, and a step prices the lift from changeover, overtime and expedite costs in your own books.

The plant manager said most late orders are parts shortages, and the example ignored material. The example now feeds material arrival dates. The fixed 2-day freeze read as a rule, so it is now a suggested starting point. Vendor cases stay labelled, with the NIST case first.

Steve wanted to know where his data would live and what the 30 minutes buys. The tools table now says EDGEBIC runs on your own PCs, not in the cloud. The offer now promises the first step, a before-and-after measure and the data to fix first, with no sales pitch.

answers.human-role: Your planner approves every schedule before release and can override any move, with the reason logged.[^4][^2] Supervisors confirm what the floor can run, and the operations manager sets the rules the software follows.[^9][^15]
answers.team-after: Planners stop building the schedule by hand and work exceptions instead: late orders, material gaps, what-ifs and what to tell customers.[^9][^19]
answers.example: The software proposes a new sequence, moves the down machine's jobs to other machines, and costs the fixes. The planner picks one and releases it.[^16][^21][^4]
answers.table-1: Small shops fit ERP schedulers such as Business Central, Odoo or MRPeasy. Plants with many changeovers fit stand-alone schedulers such as SkyPlanner, EDGEBIC or PlanetTogether.[^25][^7][^24][^29][^8][^30] Plants with unusual rules can build on frePPLe or a free solver.[^32][^41]
answers.table-2: The one independent case, from NIST MEP, cut lead time from 12-14 weeks to 5 after fixing routings first. Vendor cases claim gains such as 25% fewer changeovers.[^36]
answers.recipes: Small shops fit their ERP's own scheduler, plants with many changeovers fit a stand-alone scheduler, and data-rich plants with unusual rules can build on a free solver.[^41]
answers.own-data: By our math, year-one list licenses for a 100-person shop ran from about $2,940 (MRPeasy Starter) to a $25,000 one-time license (EDGEBIC).[^24][^8] Five of 12 tools publish no usable price.[^30][^31][^45][^34][^33]
answers.rules: The EU AI Act makes AI that assigns tasks to workers high-risk from 2 Dec 2027, and Chicago's Fair Workweek Ordinance requires 14 days' shift notice.[^47][^49] Neither covers sequencing machines alone.
answers.benchmark: Freeze the data from 4-6 past weeks with real disruptions, replay them in the tool, and compare against what happened and a simple earliest-due-date rule.[^39] Count every capacity or calendar violation, then run 4 weeks in shadow with the planner approving.[^5][^4]
answers.what-goes-wrong: Production scheduling software goes wrong through bad master data, shadow spreadsheets, planners losing their say, schedule churn, wrong shift calendars and untested vendor claims.[^4][^51][^1][^21][^13][^22]
answers.something-else: Pick something else when one bottleneck drives everything, demand is steady and repeats, material drives lead times, or your routings and run times are wrong.[^54][^55][^56][^57] Drum-Buffer-Rope, kanban, DDMRP or a NIST MEP center may fit better.
